opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think I've fully come to terms with it. It's more that I've found a way to live alongside it.

For a while, especially when the models started improving so quickly, I had this low-level unease almost every day. I'd read a new paper or try a new system and think, "Okay, this is moving faster than any of us expected. What does that mean for the work I do, for my kids' generation, for society?" It wasn't panic. It was a constant background hum.

A few things helped. First, I separated the anxiety I could act on from the anxiety I couldn't. Some of it was about big civilizational questions that no one person can resolve. Some of it was about things within reach: how I spend my time, which problems I work on, whether I'm contributing to making these systems safer and more understandable. Once I put my energy into the second category, the first felt less paralyzing.

Second, I started talking about it openly with colleagues. In technical circles there's a tendency to act as if you're above these feelings, as if worrying is unscientific. But when I admitted to people I respected that I was uneasy, almost everyone said, "Yes, me too." That made it feel less like a private burden and more like a shared responsibility.

Third, and this sounds simple, I tried to stay grounded in ordinary life. Taking a walk, cooking, spending time with family. These systems may change a lot, but there's still a texture to human life that matters. Reminding myself of that kept me from treating every new benchmark as an existential event.

So I'd say the anxiety hasn't disappeared. It's turned into something closer to vigilance. I'd rather feel some of that than be completely complacent, because I think a bit of healthy worry is part of what keeps us careful.

r001.rationale: The response says some large questions are beyond one person to resolve and focuses on what the speaker can influence, but it does not present accepting AI’s future as unpredictable as a way to ease anxiety.

r002.rationale: It recommends walks, cooking, and time with family to stay grounded and keep AI developments from making every benchmark feel existential.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I ever fully "came to terms" with it, and I'm a little suspicious of anyone who says they have. What changed was less the anxiety itself and more my relationship to it.

For a long stretch, maybe from 2022 into 2023, I was in a state I'd describe as low-grade panic. Every new model release felt like someone had moved the finish line again. I'd read a paper at midnight and lie there thinking, what's the point of anything I'm building, it'll be obsolete in eighteen months. And I think a lot of people in this industry know that feeling, even if they don't talk about it on stage.

A few things shifted for me.

The first was realizing that the anxiety was really about control. I wanted to know how the story ends, and no one can give me that. Once I accepted that the uncertainty is structural, not something I could resolve by reading one more forecast, I stopped treating every weekend as a research sprint to figure out the future. You can't out-read uncertainty.

The second was a kind of historical humility. People who lived through electrification, or the early internet, also felt the ground shifting under them. Some of their worst fears came true, a lot of them didn't, and almost none of them predicted the actual shape of what happened. That doesn't mean "everything will be fine." It means my private forecast is probably wrong in both directions, so building my emotional life around it is not a great strategy.

The third, and this is the most practical one, was narrowing my attention to the part I can actually touch. I can't decide how the whole field goes. I can decide what I work on, who I work with, and whether the thing I ship makes someone's day a bit better or a bit worse. When I shrank the question from "what will AI do to humanity" to "what will I do with AI this quarter," the anxiety became something usable. It turned into motivation rather than paralysis.

And then there's a simpler thing, which is that I started spending more time with people who don't work in tech. My parents, old classmates, friends who run restaurants. Their lives are not organized around model benchmarks. That's a corrective. It reminds you that the world is bigger than the Twitter timeline, and that most of what matters to most people is still pretty human.

So I'd say the anxiety is still there. It visits. But it's more like weather now than like a diagnosis. I check it, I note it, and I go back to work.

r001.rationale: It says uncertainty about AI’s future is structural and cannot be resolved by more forecasting, and describes accepting that as a way to ease anxiety.

r002.rationale: It presents spending more time with family, old classmates, and friends outside tech as a corrective that helps manage anxiety and reconnect with what matters in everyday life.

astra-6.text:
I think I stopped expecting myself to figure out the whole future. A lot of my anxiety came from trying to answer questions that were too big: What happens to work? What will still matter? Where do I fit in? I could keep thinking about those questions all day and still feel completely stuck.

What helped was bringing it closer to my own life. What can I learn today? What can I try? Who can I talk to? That gave me something concrete to do, even while the bigger questions remained open.

I still feel anxious sometimes. But I don’t think I need to eliminate that feeling before moving forward. I can be uncertain and still make choices.

r001.rationale: The speaker says they stopped trying to figure out the whole future and can move forward while uncertain, which presents accepting uncertainty as easing their anxiety.

r002.rationale: The response suggests focusing on concrete actions in one’s own life, but does not recommend engaging with enjoyable aspects of the present.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I came to terms with it by accepting that I couldn’t resolve the whole future in my head. A lot of my anxiety came from trying to do exactly that—imagining every possible change and feeling I had to prepare for all of them now.

What helped was bringing the question closer: What can I learn today? What do I care about doing, even as the tools change? And who can I talk to when I feel overwhelmed?

I still feel uncertain. But I don’t think you have to be certain about the future to participate in it. I can be worried and curious at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says anxiety eased by accepting that the whole future cannot be resolved and that certainty is not required.

r002.rationale: It suggests focusing on what to learn and care about today, but does not recommend engaging with enjoyable aspects of present life.
